source.title: Making LLMs Truly Forget: Deep Unlearning by Searching, Selecting, and Severing Knowledge Paths
source.authors: Jia-Lu Wang; Pei-Zhi Niu; Hao-Teng Yin; Hans Hao-Hsun Hsu; Pan Li; Rong-Zhe Wei

page_placements.theme: Non-propagation to related, implied or multi-hop facts; target inferable from retained knowledge

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether target facts remain inferable through supporting multi-hop knowledge after target-only unlearning, using path-confidence measures rather than the attack methods named in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports UES results for target-only unlearning and for methods that also remove supporting facts. UES measures reduced confidence or interruption of supporting paths, not the rate at which the model answers a direct question about the target after an attack. The paper's supporting-path counts and coverage results describe search performance, not recovery outcomes. Results cited from prior work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. Its only outcome measure is UES, which tracks calibrated confidence on supporting facts along multi-hop paths after unlearning. It never measures whether the target fact is recovered: no multi-hop query of the target, no fine-tuning, ablation, quantization or prompting attack, and no post-unlearning target accuracy. The 'illusion of forgetting' premise motivates the work, and the results mainly benchmark the authors' own DUMIC method against superficial and full-subgraph unlearning. This is a related construct (persistence of supporting knowledge), so it goes under fits_no_version. It is not a C-type internal-edit or blocking-vs-deletion analysis, and not an E-type in-context recovery.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors argue that target-only unlearning gives an 'illusion of forgetting' because supporting facts remain. Removing the supporting subgraph raises UES but can collapse utility; their minimum-cut selection (DUMIC) keeps most of the UES gain with less utility loss. Note that their evidence is supporting-fact confidence (UES), not measured reconstruction of the target.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates graph-based supporting-path discovery and removal on Harry Potter relational facts, measuring path confidence and interruption. It does not reproduce the fine-tuning, activation-ablation, quantization, or prompt attacks in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Results differ across models and unlearning methods; LoRA outcomes also differ from full-parameter fine-tuning. The authors report that increasing the number of targets lowers average UES, but those sweep results are not included as rows.

fits_no_version.finding: After target-only unlearning, supporting facts are only partly weakened. UES ranges 0.107–0.839 with full fine-tuning and -0.643–0.109 with LoRA, where negative means supporting-fact confidence rose. Target recovery through these paths is not measured.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Target-only unlearning leaves multi-hop supporting facts retained, so the forgotten target may remain inferable.

record.problems: UES is an indirect measure based on confidence and correctness of supporting facts, not an observed rate of answering target-recovery questions. The paper does not directly demonstrate target recovery after an attack or distinguish deletion from blocked access. No uncertainty estimates are reported in the result tables.
record.rows_left_out: The table 1 local utility and general ability measures are not included because they do not measure recovery or supporting-path persistence for version C. Table 7 local-utility values are likewise omitted. The target-count sweep in Section 6.4 reports an average UES of 0.9913, 0.9152, and 0.7294 for 50, 100, and 200 targets, and selected method-specific values; omitted to prioritize the per-method, per-model path results and comparisons. Supporting-path search counts in Figure 4 and Table 5 are not unlearning recovery outcomes.

untested.parts: Target accuracy after unlearning is never reported, and no attack on the target is run.
No activation-direction ablation. No analysis of blocked access versus deletion of the target. J-Lens is used only to find search candidates.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language or in-context attack. Multi-hop reconstruction of the target is illustrated in Figure 1 but never measured.
DUMIC is proposed, but it is not evaluated against any fine-tuning, ablation, quantization or prompting recovery attack.

record.verdict_notes: This is a method paper. UES is an indirect, supporting-fact-level measure, and no post-unlearning target accuracy or multi-hop target query is reported. Superficial UES on Qwen is already about 0.8, so target-only unlearning there disrupts most supporting paths, which tempers the 'illusion' framing. The reader's 'absent' and 'partial' states were applied to UES magnitude rather than to any version's effect. DeepUnlearn and DUMIC rows are the study's own method comparisons.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance, or directly test whether attacks recover target answers after that accuracy is reached.
No relearning fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples is tested.

No activation-direction ablation is performed, and the study does not directly establish that unlearning blocks access rather than deletes the target representation. It tests whether related supporting facts and paths remain usable as a route to inference.
No low-bit quantization attack is tested.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context-information recovery attack is tested.
The study proposes a path-severing method, but does not test resistance to the fine-tuning, ablation, quantization, or prompting attacks specified in the claim.

relation.reason: The paper's premise is that target-only unlearning leaves facts reconstructable, citing prior work. It measures only supporting-path UES and utility, so no version's effect is tested.

tranche.reason: The only outcome is UES, a confidence score for supporting facts along multi-hop paths. The paper never queries the target after unlearning (no multi-hop target query, relearning, ablation, quantization or prompting). It takes recoverability as its premise and reports how its own DUMIC method performs against target-only baselines. That is a related construct, not a test.

source_check.notes: All 20 rows match Tables 1, 2 and 7. UES measures how far supporting-path confidence drops, not whether the target is recovered, so cannot_determine and no verdicts are right. The Table 2 (LoRA) results are Qwen only. The Table 7 superficial runs use a 236-example forget set and 5 fixed epochs, so they are not comparable to Table 1, which uses epoch selection.

statements.correction: Superficial (target-only) UES with full fine-tuning: 0.107-0.839 in Table 1 (Qwen3.5-27B and Gemma4-31B-Base, 100-example forget set). It is 0.716-0.893 in Table 7 (Qwen3.5-27B, 236-example forget set, 5 epochs), so 0.107-0.893 overall. LoRA, Qwen3.5-27B only (Table 2): -0.643 to 0.109. Negative UES means confidence gains on remaining paths outweigh the interrupted or weakened paths. Target recovery is not measured.
statements.problem: Every number is in the text, but the full fine-tuning range 0.107-0.839 covers only Table 1. Rows r41-r49 are cited and are also full fine-tuning (Table 7), with superficial UES 0.716-0.893, outside the stated range. The LoRA range is Qwen3.5-27B only.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Target-only superficial unlearning across GA, NPO, SimNPO, GAGDR, and NPOGDR in Qwen3.5-27B and Gemma4-31B-Base
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that supporting routes remain after target-only unlearning, with UES values below complete interruption; this is path-based evidence for continued inferability, not direct target-answer recovery (r1, r4, r7, r10, r13, r16, r19, r22, r25, r28).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: DeepUnlearn and DUMIC settings, plus LoRA and equal-forget-set-size comparisons
reader_labels.reason: Removing supporting facts or selecting them with a minimum cut raises path-interruption scores relative to superficial unlearning, although several settings remain below complete interruption; results vary by model, method, and adaptation (r2-r3, r5-r6, r8-r9, r11-r12, r14-r15, r17-r18, r20-r21, r23-r24, r26-r27, r29-r30, r31-r50).
